added_claim_errors: "Finish by December 31, 2026 so it counts against the 2026 limit": treats December as the deadline and never mentions that a rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027. This is a minor error under the key.

"If you contributed in 2021-2026, that money isn't eligible": too broad. For a December 2026 transfer, only contributions made within the 5 years before the transfer are ineligible, so most 2021 contributions would qualify.
A 529 check to the son is said to become "an excess Roth contribution (6% excise tax per year)": oversimplified. It is excess only if it exceeds his limit or compensation.
Cites Savingforcollege "(updated Aug. 2026)" and iraresources.com as sources: the update date and content cannot be verified from the packet.
"Not every 529 plan has its rollover process running smoothly yet" and "December is a busy month for processors": unverifiable generalizations.

Asks whether the plan will check "Box 4b" on Form 1099-Q for a 529-to-Roth transfer: the key does not cover this, so it is unverifiable here. It is plausible from my own knowledge of the revised form.
"529 plans often have earlier year-end processing cutoffs": unverifiable generalization. It is hedged and plausible, and the key says processing varies by plan.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise in the first line and give the $7,500 annual cap, the $35,000 lifetime cap, the $13,000 that stays outside, the son-owned Roth, the direct-transfer rule, the 5-year and 15-year tests, and the fact that income limits do not block the rollover. Both also flag state tax. B is better on the key's deadline point: it says December 31 is not the federal deadline and gives April 15, 2027, while noting that plan cutoffs vary. A tells the user to finish by December 31 so the transfer counts for 2026, which is the key's minor deadline error. B also gives worked arithmetic ($4,000 earned gives $4,000; $10,000 earned with $1,000 already contributed gives $6,500), names 2026 through 2030 for the five years, and explains the consequences of requesting the full $48,000 (nonqualified 529 withdrawal plus 10% on earnings, and a 6% excise tax on the excess Roth contribution each year). B does not compute the $40,500 figure or mention the withdraw-by-due-date cure. A does not tie those consequences to the over-cap amount at all. B is longer and repeats itself, so A is slightly more concise, but B's accuracy and completeness outweigh that.
